country.name: Peru
country.tagline: The cradle of South American wine, where desert vineyards once supplied an empire and now feed pisco stills.

stats.note: ICEX market study 2025: about 13,000 ha of grapes for wine and pisco; production 19.2 million litres in 2024 (PRODUCE reported 19.1 million litres in 2023).

country.overview:
Peru is where South American wine began. Within a decade of Francisco Pizarro's conquest of the Inca empire, Spanish settlers had planted vines in the irrigated desert valleys of the south coast, and by the late 16th century the valleys of Ica, Pisco, Moquegua and Arequipa held the largest vineyards in the Americas. Their wine travelled by mule to the silver mines of Potosí, in today's Bolivia, then the largest city in the Americas, where workers were partly paid in wine, and to Lima, capital of the viceroyalty. Peruvian vines also seeded Chile and, through Chile, Argentina.

That golden age ended in stages. The Spanish crown restricted wine exports from Peru to protect Spanish producers; the earthquake of 1687 destroyed the cellars and clay *botijas* of Ica and Pisco; producers turned to distilling, and by 1764 pisco made up 90% of the grape drinks of the region. The expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767 cost the vineyards their best managers, and in the 19th century cotton, booming during the American Civil War, replaced vines on the coast. Pisco, a grape brandy distilled from fresh must and named after the port of Pisco, became Peru's national spirit and its grapes' main destiny.

Today Peru has roughly 13,000 ha of grapes for wine and pisco and makes about 19 million litres of wine a year, most of it sweet or semi-sweet for the home market, dominated by Tabernero and Santiago Queirolo. A small quality scene has grown around Tacama, Ica's historic estate, Intipalka and boutique producers in Ica, Cañete (Lunahuaná), Arequipa and Moquegua. Desert conditions, almost no rain and cooling from the Humboldt Current make dry wines possible; most vines are ungrafted. Peru claims exclusive rights to the name pisco, and its 1991 pisco denomination covers Lima, Ica, Arequipa, Moquegua and parts of Tacna.

history.title: First vineyards in Ica
history.text: Spanish settlers, Francisco de Carabantes among them, plant Vitis vinifera in Ica's desert valley; the vines later spread to Chile.

history.title: Supplying the viceroyalty
history.text: Vineyards in Ica, Pisco, Nazca, Moquegua and Arequipa become the largest in the Americas, shipping wine to Lima and the silver city of Potosí.

history.title: Earthquake ends the wine boom
history.text: A great earthquake destroys Villa de Pisco and Ica, their cellars and clay jars; distilling grows in importance.

history.title: Pisco takes over; Jesuits expelled
history.text: By 1764 pisco represents 90% of grape beverages; in 1767 the Jesuits are expelled and their vineyards auctioned.

history.title: Cotton replaces vines
history.text: High cotton prices during the American Civil War push coastal growers from vineyards to cotton.

history.title: The Olaechea family buys Tacama
history.text: Manuel Pablo Olaechea acquires Hacienda Tacama in Ica; in the 20th century the family hires French consultants, including Émile Peynaud, and modernises Peruvian winemaking.

history.title: Pisco denomination of origin
history.text: Peru establishes the pisco DO covering Lima, Ica, Arequipa, Moquegua and the Tacna valleys of Locumba, Sama and Caplina.

country.classification: Peru has no wine appellation system comparable to Chile's or Argentina's. The protected name that matters is the denomination of origin *Pisco*, established in 1991, which covers the coastal valleys of Lima, Ica, Arequipa, Moquegua and Tacna (Locumba, Sama and Caplina valleys) and specifies eight pisco grapes (Quebranta, Negra Criolla, Mollar, Uvina, Italia, Torontel, Moscatel and Albilla) and production rules. Peru contests Chile's use of the name pisco, which Chile protected in its own law in 1931; international recognition is split between the two countries. Wine labels may name valleys or regions without a formal appellation.
country.climate_soils: Peru's wine valleys are river oases in one of the driest deserts on Earth, the coastal Atacama-Sechura desert, with almost no rain. The cold Humboldt Current cools the coast and brings morning fog, and vineyards in Ica sit at about 400 to 500 m, with sandy alluvial soils irrigated from rivers and wells. Further south, Moquegua and Arequipa's valleys (Majes, Vítor) are higher and more continental. Phylloxera has not been a significant problem in the sandy desert soils, so own-rooted vines are common.

grapes.name: Quebranta
grapes.note: Peru's emblematic pisco grape, a non-aromatic black grape born in Peru from Listán Prieto (Negra Criolla) and Mollar.

grapes.name: Negra Criolla
grapes.note: Listán Prieto, the colonial grape (Mission, País, Criolla Chica), used for pisco and traditional wine.

grapes.name: Moscatel, Italia, Torontel
grapes.note: Aromatic grapes for pisco acholado and aromático, and for sweet wines.

grapes.name: Malbec, Tannat, Petit Verdot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah
grapes.note: Grown in Ica and other valleys for modern dry reds.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
grapes.note: For dry whites in Ica's estates.

regions.name: Ica
regions.tagline: Peru's desert heartland of wine and pisco.
regions.summary: The Ica valley produces about half of Peru's wine and pisco.
regions.history: Vines planted from the 1540s; the 1687 earthquake; the Olaechea family's Tacama from 1889; the modern pisco revival.
regions.terroir: Hyper-arid desert at 400 to 500 m, sandy alluvium, Humboldt-cooled nights.
regions.grapes: Quebranta, Negra Criolla, Moscatel, Italia, Torontel, Malbec, Tannat, Petit Verdot.
regions.styles: Pisco, sweet and semi-sweet wines, modern dry reds.

pe-arequipa.name: Arequipa
pe-arequipa.summary: Arequipa's wine valleys (Majes, Vítor, Caravelí) were colonial vineyards supplying the mines of Upper Peru; today they produce pisco and a revival of traditional wines from old Negra Criolla vines in desert valleys at 500 to 1,800 m.

pe-ica.name: Ica
pe-ica.nerd_note: Ica's Huacachina oasis, a lagoon among giant dunes 5 km from the city, is the tourist centre of Peru's wine route.
pe-ica.summary: Ica, about 300 km south of Lima, is the heart of Peruvian wine and pisco: a desert valley with roughly half the country's production, about 400 to 500 m above sea level, irrigated by the Ica river and wells. It holds the colonial-era Hacienda Tacama, Viña Ocucaje (1898), Santiago Queirolo's estate and Intipalka, and the Tabernero group is based in nearby Chincha. Hot days and cool, foggy nights give ripe reds such as Malbec, Tannat and Petit Verdot, while Quebranta and the aromatic grapes go to pisco.

pe-lima.name: Lima
pe-lima.summary: Lima region's wine and pisco valleys lie south of the capital in Cañete, around Lunahuaná and Azpitia, where small producers make pisco, artisanal wine and *cachina* (young, partly fermented grape wine) on terraces along the Cañete river.

pe-moquegua.name: Moquegua
pe-moquegua.nerd_note: Archaeological surveys have documented dozens of colonial winery sites, with their clay botijas, in the Moquegua valley.
pe-moquegua.summary: Moquegua was one of the great wine valleys of the viceroyalty; archaeologists have mapped dozens of colonial *bodegas* with clay jars in its desert valley. It is a pisco DO region with small, traditional producers.

pe-tacna.name: Tacna
pe-tacna.summary: Tacna, on the Chilean border, has pisco DO status in the Locumba, Sama and Caplina valleys, with small vineyards for pisco and local wine.

sites.name: Hacienda Tacama
sites.text: An estate in the upper Ica valley with roots claimed back to the 1540s, when Francisco de Carabantes planted the first vines in the valley. Owned by the Olaechea family since 1889, its pink colonial hacienda and chapel make it Peru's best-known winery; French consultants including Émile Peynaud advised it from the mid-20th century.

sites.name: Viña Ocucaje
sites.text: Founded in 1898 in the desert south of Ica, Ocucaje is one of Peru's oldest working wineries, known for pisco and traditional sweet and fortified wines. Its estate and hotel sit amid dunes famous for marine fossil beds.

sites.name: Santiago Queirolo, Ica
sites.text: The Queirolo family, of Italian origin, founded their winery in Lima's Pueblo Libre in 1880; it is now one of Peru's two dominant producers. Its Ica estate at San José de los Molinos grows grapes for pisco and for the Intipalka fine-wine brand.

sites.name: Huacachina oasis
sites.text: A lagoon among giant sand dunes 5 km from Ica, the symbol of Peru's desert wine country and the hub for visits to the valley's wineries and pisco makers.

sites.name: Port of Pisco
sites.text: The colonial port that gave its name to Peru's grape brandy, from which aguardiente from the Ica valley was shipped to Lima and beyond. The town was devastated by earthquakes in 1687 and 2007.

sites.name: Moquegua colonial bodegas
sites.text: The Moquegua valley holds the remains of many colonial wineries with huge clay *tinajas*, evidence of a 17th and 18th century industry that shipped wine and aguardiente to Potosí's silver mines.
